title.en: 19th century reformers: Vidyasagar, Arya Samaj, Prarthana Samaj

text.en: A child widow, a ban on remarriage, a custom nobody dared question: in the 19th century some Indians began to ask whether these practices were really part of their faith. Education, printing and new ideas gave them the courage to speak and to build societies for change.

Iswar Chandra Vidyasagar campaigned for the remarriage of widows, which led to the Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856, and he promoted the education of girls.
The first age of consent was included in the Indian Penal Code of 1860 and the marriage age was later raised, but the law often remained on paper.
Swami Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 in Punjab; his book Satyarthaprakash spread its ideas and his cry was go back to the Vedas.
He rejected child marriage, idolatry and Brahman domination of ritual, and stood for strict monotheism.
Arya Samaj prescribed a purificatory ceremony called suddhi for Hindus who had converted.
The Prarthana Samaj was founded in Bombay in 1867 by Dr Atma Ram Pandurang; R.C. Bhandarkar and Justice M.G. Ranade worked for inter-caste dining, inter-caste marriage, widow remarriage and women's improvement.
These movements combined reason, education and social service to reform society and prepared the ground for later nationalism.

problem.en: Why did reformers insist that a custom like banning widow remarriage had no support in scripture?

text.en: People defend customs by saying they are sacred.
Showing that the old texts do not require it removes the excuse.

why.en: That was Dayanand's and Vidyasagar's argument.

text.en: Then law and education can change the practice.

why.en: Reform needs both ideas and law.

prompt.en: Name two reformers and one reform they achieved.

commonMisconceptions.en: Confusing Arya Samaj with Brahmo Samaj

Reform needed both new ideas and new laws.
